title: Rate-Amplifying Demand and the Excess Sensitivity of Long-Term Rates

source.name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

summary: This Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Report (Number 810, revised April 2021) by Hanson, Lucca, and Wright documents a puzzling post-2000 shift in the relationship between short- and long-term interest rates: high-frequency sensitivity of long rates to short rates has strengthened while low-frequency sensitivity has weakened. The paper explains this pattern through a model where rate declines trigger 'rate-amplifying' demand shifts for long-term bonds, and arbitrage is limited and slow.
key_points: Long-term nominal interest rates exhibit excess sensitivity to high-frequency (daily or monthly) movements in short-term rates, and this sensitivity has grown stronger since 2000
Low-frequency association (6- or 12-month horizons) between long- and short-term rates was strong pre-2000 but has weakened substantially since
The mechanism: increases in short rates temporarily raise the term premium component of long-term yields, causing long rates to overreact to short rate changes
Rate-amplifying demand is traced to three sources: mortgage refinancing activity, investors who extrapolate recent short-rate changes, and investors who 'reach for yield' when short rates fall
Arbitrage response to these demand shifts is both limited and slow, allowing the mispricing to persist
Paper discusses implications for event-study methodologies and monetary policy transmission
why_it_matters: This research challenges simple expectations hypotheses of the term structure and has direct implications for how monetary policy moves through financial markets. If long-term rates overreact to short-rate changes due to investor behavior (refinancing, extrapolation, reach for yield), then policy announcements may have larger-than-expected effects on yields. The findings also suggest that event-study approaches that assume rapid arbitrage may mismeasure policy impacts.
market_structure_context: The paper directly addresses market structure by analyzing term premium dynamics, investor demand functions for long-duration bonds, and the speed/limits of arbitrage in the Treasury market. Key mechanisms include mortgage refinancing pipelines (which create demand when rates fall), extrapolative expectations among bond investors, and reach-for-yield behavior that amplifies rate moves.
